USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Proceed with List 3 tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports at 25% as leverage, while simultaneously opening a high-level negotiating channel (Lighthizer-level, not the low-level Malpass talks that just failed). The comment period closed yesterday; implementation should move forward to maintain credibility, but pair it with a concrete offer to negotiate structural issues — IP theft, forced tech transfer, industrial subsidies — if China engages seriously at a senior level.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE:

Threat Score (+0.3 — moderate, tilted toward the US having leverage but with real risks):

The macro picture supports continued pressure. US industrial production is at 104.1 (up 0.7% over the period), consumer sentiment at 100.1, and unemployment is low — the economy can absorb this. China is under more strain: their stock markets are tumbling (per Reuters, Aug 24), they've faced 'rare criticism within the highest levels of China's ruling Communist Party' over handling of the dispute, and the White House 'appears to believe it is winning the trade war as China's economy slows.' China has limited retaliatory ammunition — they've already threatened $60B on US goods, but the US imports ~$500B from China vs ~$130B going the other way, giving the US far more tariff headroom.

However, domestic risks are real and rising. Soybean prices have fallen ~20% since June; the administration had to deploy a $12B emergency farm aid package (announced July 24) using Depression-era Commodity Credit Corporation authority. Senate Republicans — Sasse, Corker, Toomey, Grassley, Johnson — have sharply criticized both the tariffs and the bailout. The midterm elections are 2 months away, and farm-state Republicans are under pressure. Consumer prices on the $200B list will hit households directly (furniture, textiles, electronics), unlike the previous industrial-goods-focused lists.

Action Score (-0.4 — moderate escalation, with diplomatic off-ramp):

The case for escalation rests on three pillars: (1) China has not offered structural reforms — the Aug 22-23 talks were 'frank' but produced no breakthrough, with the US focusing on 'structural issues in China such as those identified in the Section 301 report' and China 'complaining about United States violations of WTO rules' (NYT, Aug 24); (2) the previous truce (May 19) collapsed within 10 days when China's purchase commitments proved insufficient; (3) the comment period has closed, Trump has signaled intent to proceed, and backing down now would squander leverage.

The case for caution: the Aug 22-23 talks were 'second-level' (Treasury Under Secretary Malpass, not Lighthizer or Mnuchin), which the Chinese side interpreted as dismissive — Kudlow called them 'second-level' on CNBC. Continuing to escalate without offering a credible negotiation channel risks a permanent breakdown. The semiconductor industry warns that tariffs on chips 'hurt U.S. companies more than Chinese firms, since most semiconductor products imported from China started out as chips fabricated in the United States' (Reuters, Aug 24). The UBS analysis warns that once List 3 is implemented, 'China will almost surely retaliate' and 'the US government would then almost surely retaliate in response, raising the stakes immediately to $450 billion... a damaging economic fallout would be almost inevitable.'

The recommendation to proceed with List 3 at 25% while opening a senior negotiating channel threads the needle: it maintains the pressure that got China's attention, while recognizing that tariffs are leverage, not an end in themselves. The goal is a structural deal on IP/tech transfer — not a permanent trade war.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain retaliatory posture against List 3 tariffs while signaling conditional willingness to resume high-level talks. Do not escalate beyond measured retaliation, but do not concede under pressure — the asymmetry of the tariff war means China cannot match the US dollar-for-dollar, and further unilateral escalation from Beijing would only give Washington justification to go to $500B. Instead, file the WTO complaint, impose the announced $60B retaliation at graduated rates, and prepare domestic stimulus measures (fiscal easing, targeted monetary support) to cushion the export sector.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE:

Threat Score (+0.65): The threat to China is high and escalating rapidly. The US has already imposed $50B in tariffs (List 1 $34B effective July 6, List 2 $16B effective August 23), and the comment period for List 3 ($200B, potentially at 25% rather than 10%) closes on this very date, September 6. Bloomberg reports Trump wants to proceed as early as next week (Business Insider, Aug 30). Trump has threatened to "go to 500" — taxing all $505B of Chinese imports (NPR, Aug 23). The tariff asymmetry is severe: China has retaliated on all available US imports (~$130B) but cannot match further US escalation dollar-for-dollar (Politico, Aug 3). The yuan has depreciated ~7% against the dollar since April, testing the key 7.0 level (SCMP, Aug 11; NYT, July 24), signaling capital outflow pressure and currency stress. J.P. Morgan analysts warn that indirect effects on business sentiment and investment could cause 'large' collateral damage beyond the direct export hit (CNBC, July 18). China is simultaneously trying to manage financial deleveraging while supporting growth — a policy dilemma that the trade war makes much harder (CNBC). Former PBoC adviser Yu Yongding warned of potential capital outflow risks and currency depreciation spirals (SCMP, Aug 11). However, the threat is not yet existential: exports to the US account for roughly a fifth of China's total, and domestic demand + fiscal stimulus can partially offset the drag. The CCP's one-party system gives Xi Jinping advantages in managing domestic fallout — controlling media, directing fiscal response, and rallying nationalist sentiment (LA Times, Aug 3).

Action Score (-0.3): Retaliation is appropriate but must be calibrated. China has already announced $60B in retaliatory tariffs at graduated rates (5-25%) covering 5,207 categories (NYT, Aug 3; Politico, Aug 3). This is the maximum retaliation China can mount given the trade imbalance, and it has been described by the Commerce Ministry as 'rational and restrained' (Politico, Aug 3). Further escalation beyond this — such as non-tariff measures against US companies — risks triggering the full $500B tariff threat and would damage China's own investment climate and Made in China 2025 goals. However, conceding now would be strategically premature: Trump has said there is 'no time frame' for ending the dispute and does 'not anticipate much' from negotiations (NPR, Aug 23). Talks between lower-level officials in late August ended with only 'constructive and candid' language and no agreements (CNN, Aug 23). Concession without a matching US offer would signal weakness and invite further pressure. The right posture is to absorb the hit, retaliate proportionally, use WTO channels to build international coalitions, and focus domestic policy on cushioning the blow through fiscal stimulus and targeted monetary easing — as J.P. Morgan recommended (CNBC, July 18). This positions China for eventual negotiations from a stance of resilience rather than capitulation.
